App name vs subtitle vs keywords vs description

App Store Connect treats each zh-Hans field as a separate job. The app name is the bold title line in Search and on the product page — Apple commonly caps it at 30 characters for zh-Hans (verify in Connect before you save). Everything else sits below or beside it:

  • Subtitle — ~30 visible characters under the app name. Not the name field.
  • Keywords — hidden 100-character field. Search variants belong here, not stuffed into the name.
  • Description — long listing body buyers expand. Not the name.
  • Promotional text & What's New — time-limited or version-specific slots. Not the name.

This page covers app name rewrite only. For subtitle work, see our Simplified Chinese subtitle guide. For keywords, see our keywords guide. For full listing fields together, see our China storefront listing guide.

Why English-only app names fail on the China storefront

US and EU indie teams often add a zh-Hans localization row but leave the app name identical to en-US. On the China storefront that reads as half-localized — and Search behavior punishes it in ways subtitle copy cannot fix:

  • Search intent mismatch — Chinese users type category nouns and problem phrases in Simplified Chinese. An English-only name does not match those queries.
  • Skim-trust signal — a roman-letter name above Chinese screenshots tells buyers the team did not finish localization.
  • Character budget wasted — 30 zh-Hans characters can carry brand plus category; 30 English letters often spell only a coined brand with no searchable meaning.
  • Competitor confusion — generic English names (“Focus”, “Flow”, “Note”) collide with dozens of unrelated apps in both locales.

Fixing subtitle and description without touching the name leaves the highest-weight visible field English-only. Better zh-Hans app names improve clarity and Search relevance — they do not replace subtitle, keyword, or description work.

30 characters — and why Chinese packs more meaning per character

Apple’s app name limit is commonly 30 characters for zh-Hans — the same cap as en-US, but the information density differs. One Simplified Chinese morpheme often equals a full English word or phrase:

  • English — “Pomodoro Focus Timer” burns 21 characters before you add a brand name.
  • zh-Hans — “番茄钟专注” (four characters) states category and workflow; remaining budget can hold a short brand or audience tag.
  • Compound nouns — “发票扫描” (invoice scan), “习惯打卡” (habit check-in), “白噪音助眠” (white noise sleep) fit category plus outcome in under ten characters.

Strong zh-Hans names use that density deliberately: keep the English brand where Chinese users expect it, then spend remaining characters on the one category noun Search needs — not on adjective stacks copied from en-US marketing decks.

Trademark and name collision risk

The app name field is where Apple and Chinese users both expect identity — and where collisions hurt most:

  • Generic English names — “Calendar Pro”, “PDF Master”, “AI Writer” overlap existing CN listings; Search may surface a competitor first.
  • Literal brand translation — translating a coined English brand into unrelated Chinese characters can read as a different product or an impersonation attempt.
  • Trademark-sensitive terms — category nouns are fair game; famous marks, competitor product names, and “官方” (official) claims without authorization create review and legal risk.
  • Duplicate naming across locales — zh-Hans and en-US names should promise the same app, but identical roman strings in both fields waste the zh-Hans character budget.

AppLocale rewrites for clarity and search intent — we do not provide trademark clearance or legal review. When your English name is a registered mark, tell us in your intake email so we preserve it correctly in zh-Hans.

Why pinyin dumps and machine translation tank search and trust

Indie teams under deadline often paste one of two shortcuts into the zh-Hans name field. Both fail for different reasons:

  • Pinyin-only names — romanizing “专注待办” as “ZhuanZhu DaiBan” wastes visible characters and does not match how Chinese users search. Pinyin helps pronunciation; it is not a substitute for category nouns.
  • Machine translation of the English name — slogan lines (“Make Life Better”) translate into formal hollow phrases (“让生活更美好”) that could describe any app.
  • Character-by-character transliteration — English brand words mapped to look-alike Chinese characters create nonsense or accidental rude meanings.
  • Keyword stuffing in the name — cramming search terms Apple expects in the keyword field into 30 visible characters reads as spam and may trigger editorial scrutiny.

Machine drafts are fine for internal notes. Finished zh-Hans app names need idiomatic phrasing that keeps your English brand voice while naming the category Chinese users actually type. AppLocale rewrites the name by hand; we do not deliver raw Google Translate or LLM output as finished copy.

What a good zh-Hans app name carries

Within 30 characters, strong Chinese app names usually combine two elements:

  • Brand anchor — keep the English product name when users already know it, or a concise Chinese brand coinage when they do not.
  • Category or outcome noun — one searchable word Chinese users type: “番茄钟”, “记账”, “扫描”, “冥想”, “待办”.
  • Audience tag (optional) — when characters remain: “学生”, “独立开发者”, “小团队”.
  • No duplicate subtitle job — pricing model and feature stacks belong in subtitle or description, not repeated in the name.

Write for a Chinese skim reader deciding which Search result to tap — not for a keyword-density checklist copied from en-US ASO blogs.

Common zh-Hans app name mistakes

  • Leaving the en-US app name unchanged on the zh-Hans localization row
  • Pasting pinyin where Chinese users expect hanzi category words
  • Translating a coined English brand into unrelated Chinese characters
  • Stuffing the name with keywords that belong in the hidden keyword field
  • Using formal false cognates (“专业级”, “高效能”) that read as template copy
  • Exceeding the 30-character limit and getting truncated mid-word in Search
  • Choosing a generic name that collides with existing CN listings in the same category

A clearer app name improves Search relevance and product-page trust — it does not replace subtitle, keyword, description, or in-app UI localization.
